study.title: Bible Study of Naum 1
study.overview: Nahum 1 presents the Lord as the sovereign Judge who rules history, punishes evil and at the same time is a refuge for those who trust in him. The chapter alternates between the threat against Nineveh and the promise of relief for Judah. The central message is that no human power can resist the judgment of God, but his people finds in him security, liberation and peace.

outline.title: Inscription of the prophecy
outline.explanation: The book is presented as a revelation against Nineveh, and identifies Naum as a bearer of this prophetic vision. The notes highlight that the name of the prophet can be understood as "comfort" or "encourajation," which combines with the effect of his message to Judah.

outline.title: The Holy Character and the Lord's Sovereign Power
outline.explanation: The poem describes God as zealous, avenger, late to anger and great in power. He dominates the creation, shakes the earth and makes the waters dry. At the same time, it is good and strong in the day of distress, knowing those who trust in him.

outline.title: The sentence against Nineveh and the end of the oppressor
outline.explanation: The plans against the Lord are useless, and Assyrian power will be consumed. The text announces the breaking of the yoke upon Judah, the end of the name and images of the Assyrian god, and the grave of the oppressor for its shame and contempt.

outline.title: Good news and peace for Judah
outline.explanation: The arrival of the messenger on the mountains announces peace: Judah can celebrate and fulfill his vows, because the evil one has been destroyed. The notes link this liberation to the end of Assyrian oppression and the hope of peace brought by God.

study.context: The notes place Nineveh as the capital of the Assyrian Empire until its destruction in 612 BC. They also relate the prophecy to Assyrian oppression over Judah and, in some readings, to the defeat of the Assyrian army in the days of Hezekiah or the period after the death of Asurbanípal. The biblical text, however, focuses less on chronological details and more on the proclamation of the divine judgment and deliverance of God's people.
study.theology: Nahum 1 teaches that the judgment of God is not whim, but an expression of his holiness, righteousness, and faithfulness to his covenant. The divine wrath against the enemies of God is not like human vengeance; it is holy and upright. At the same time, the chapter preserves the doctrine of consolation: God is good, it is stronghold in suffering and knows those who trust in it. There is also a clear emphasis on divine sovereignty over creation, nations and human projects. No conspiracy against the Lord prospers. The good news for Judah is that oppression will not have the final word: God breaks the yoke, undoes the bonds and gives peace.

scholarViews.insight: The notes see in 1:15 the arrival of a messenger with good news of peace, that is, the announcement that Assyrian dominion over Judah would be broken and the people of God would be free from their weight.
The note understands 1:15 as the announcement of messengers who bring the news of Nineveh's destruction, allowing Judah to celebrate their feasts in safety again.
The note interprets 1:15 as an allusion to the good news of the fall of Nineveh, after which Assyria would no longer pass through the land of Judah.

questions: What does this chapter teach me about the holiness of God and about the seriousness of opposing at his will?
In what situations do I need to remember that the Lord is stronghold in the day of anguish and knows those who trust in him?
What concrete signs of gratitude and obedience appear in my life when I receive the peace that God gives?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to the fear of God and to trust in him. If there are areas in which you try to control everything on your own, give them to the Lord. If you are suffering oppression, anxiety or fear, remember that God sees, knows and acts. As Judah, respond to God's deliverance with faithful worship, fulfillment of vows and practical gratitude: return to prayer, faithfulness and adoration, trusting that the evil one will not have the last word.
study.uncertainty: Notes offer interpretive historical readings, but do not place with total certainty the exact date or the specific historical event behind 1:15. There is also mention, in a note, of a broader and more Christological application of peace, but this is a later theological reading and should not be confused with the immediate meaning of the text.
